Arsenal 'have ingredients' but Europe's elite on another level

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Arsenal goalkeeper Misa Rodriguez made six saves but was beaten twice in defeat by Lyon.
  • It is only 18 months since Arsenal tasted European glory, but they are not a team on many people's list of favourites for this season's Women's Champions League.
  • That is because not only have the Gunners disappointed across their opening 15 matches of the season, but also the elite teams in Europe seem to have gone up another level.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arsenal goalkeeper Misa Rodriguez made six saves but was beaten twice in defeat by Lyon.

It is only 18 months since Arsenal tasted European glory, but they are not a team on many people's list of favourites for this season's Women's Champions League.

That is because not only have the Gunners disappointed across their opening 15 matches of the season, but also the elite teams in Europe seem to have gone up another level.

In the space of seven days, Arsenal have witnessed first hand what it takes to reach those heights - and the gap they must bridge.

Last week, they were resilient at Barcelona to earn a very respectable 1-1 draw, but were fortunate the Spanish side were not clinical with their chances at Camp Nou.

On Thursday night, they were outplayed at home in losing 2-0 to an excellent Lyon side, who look on course to match or better their runner-up finish from last season.

One point from such games could be pleasing - but that only shows the work Arsenal need to do to be considered one of the top teams in Europe.

French giants Lyon outclass Arsenal in Women's Champions League.

Arsenal came into Thursday's defeat by Lyon off the back of a fifth successive Women's Super League draw at Emirates Stadium against London City Lionesses.

In contrast, Lyon have been flying domestically, winning all nine of their matches, scoring 49 goals, and then not conceding any in their unbeaten Champions League run.

Such form sets the pace and it was clear at Meadow Park that they were superior to Arsenal in every department.

Vibrant Germany international Jule Brand gave them the lead midway through the first half and Melchie Dumornay sealed the win with a powerful strike in the 57th minute.

Arsenal defender Leah Williamson remarked the "better team won the game" and manager Renee Slegers highlighted the difference in physicality between the teams.

"Compared to last year when we played Lyon [in the semi-finals], they are even better now. They have standout individual quality," Slegers mentioned.

In a recent development, "They dominated in the first half. We had solutions for the second half and had more presence. We wore them down better but it still didn't lead to open chances.".

Despite playing at right-back, Jule Brand had the third most touches in the Arsenal penalty area for Lyon (five) after striker Marie-Antoinette Katoto and fellow goalscorer Melchie Dumornay.

It has been revealed that lyon had a 3.33 expected goals ratio on Thursday, serving up 23 shots to Arsenal's seven. They created six big chances and 14 of their shots were inside the box.

Dumornay oozed quality, midfielder Lily Yohannes demonstrated composure and Brand was very impressive both defensively and going forward for Lyon, deployed in a newly introduced position.

Those individuals have benefitted from the expertise of former Barcelona manager Jonatan Giraldez, who joined in June 2025 - the month after Arsenal won the Champions League - and has now had the time he needed to impose his style.

As a result, Lyon have gone up another level and the gap between these two teams has widened by Arsenal's drop-off this season.

Slegers also mentioned Arsenal had "prepared all we could" for the intensity that Lyon brought in London - but it still did not have an impact.

Asked how far off Lyon they right now are, Slegers said: "It's 2-0 today and they are better than us but it doesn't mean if we were to play them again soon, this season, that it would be the same game again.

"We saw moments where we did well and we know from the last couple of years we can hurt Lyon.

In a recent development, "But for today, their pace and physicality helped them get too much dominance in the game and that is one of their strengths. Then it became hard for us.".

Arsenal have not yet qualified for the knockout stages of the Champions League.

Williamson remarked Arsenal "know what they need to do to be better" and that they are aware of "where the gaps are" to Europe's elite.

They are already 12 points off the pace in the Women's Super League title race and are unlikely to qualify automatically for the Champions League quarter-finals.

"The level rises year on year. Everybody cops goals - we have to try not to and we have to create," said Williamson following the defeat by Lyon.

"We're all focused and we're all together. That's the most comforting thing for me - but this has been a tough period.".

It has not all been bad despite disappointing results - and context is crucial.

Over a gruelling seven days, they have faced European holders Barcelona, WSL high-flyers London City Lionesses and record Champions League winners Lyon.

They demonstrated grit and resilience out in Barcelona last week - traits that have not been on show enough for Arsenal this season, but are clearly there.

Players like Williamson, striker Alessia Russo and summer signings Georgia Stanway and Ona Batlle know what it takes to compete at the highest level.

Arsenal invested in the summer transfer window and brought in proven, experienced players, but that has not translated into results - yet.

Giraldez remarked time with his players has helped improve Lyon and perhaps that is what Arsenal need - patience.

It has been revealed that "I think they are changing now. They made a good game against Barcelona and it's very difficult to go there and get a point," said Giraldez.

Sources indicate that "The game against London City was much better. It's not just about them, but also about us. Now we have improved and play better football than last year.

"I think it is a matter of time [for Arsenal]. They have a good coach and good players. In general, they have all the ingredients to have a good season.".

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed.

Washington Spirit clinch third consecutive trip to NWSL Championship with win over Utah Royals

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1055 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After two runner-up finishes at the NWSL Championship, the Washington Spirit will get a third consecutive shot at lifting the massive prize.
  • The Washington Spirit rallied from an early deficit to defeat the Utah Royals 2-1 in front of another sold-out Audi Field.
  • early in the week, avoiding a nationwide flight stoppage on Friday, and fresh off a huge quarterfinal upset -- a 1-0 win against the No.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After two runner-up finishes at the NWSL Championship, the Washington Spirit will get a third consecutive shot at lifting the massive prize.

The Washington Spirit rallied from an early deficit to defeat the Utah Royals 2-1 in front of another sold-out Audi Field. The Spirit weathered the fastest goal in NWSL playoff history, then flipped the script within minutes and never took their foot off the pedal or lost control. Utah Royals' Cloe Lacasse struck first on the scoreboard, and Sofia Cantore and Clara Luvanga provided the decisive goals for the Spirit, while Trinity Rodman brought plenty of spark and Andi Sullivan supplied reliable, steady play in the midfield.

Here's how the Spirit rallied for the win:.

The Royals arrived in D.C. early in the week, avoiding a nationwide flight stoppage on Friday, and fresh off a huge quarterfinal upset -- a 1-0 win against the No. 2 seed San Diego Wave FC. They wasted little time to show their early playoff win was no fluke.

In a recent development, in the opening two minutes, Utah won a corner kick, and Lacasse created multiple moments of history. Her service into the box curled toward the near post, creating some miscommunication between goalkeeper Sandy MacIver and her defenders, and the ball snuck into the net. It was the fastest goal scored in NWSL playoff history and the first-ever olimpico scored in the postseason.

Industry observers note that CLOÉ LACASSE OLIMPICO IN THE SECOND MINUTE 😱@UtahRoyalsFC off to a FLYING start the @NWSL semifinal!Watch the action LIVE on @CBS and @paramountplus! pic.twitter.com/UfWxDcSB5Y.

Sources indicate that the early breakthrough stunned the typically rowdy crowd, though the set-piece tally was hardly a surprise, considering Utah's ability this year. The squad scored 15 goals off set pieces this season, with seven headed goals, so Lacasse's ability to score from the flag was just one more highlight for its set-piece playbook.

The early lead should have been a boost for the visiting side, but instead, it opened up the game; the Spirit then tested the Royals with relentless attacking pressure.

In a recent development, the Spirit needed just six minutes to turn things around. Washington's attacking trio combined for the equalizer, with Luvanga finding Rodman out wide in space, and the winger promptly connecting with Cantore in front of goal.

SOFIA CANTORE WITH THE BACKHEEL 🤯Her seventh goal of 2026 is her first playoff goal to bring @WashSpirit level 1-1!Watch the action LIVE on @CBS and @paramountplus! pic.twitter.com/C8J63tVzQn.

"I think getting scored on in the first few minutes will really humble you, and a little bit of a wake-up call, but I thought our response was incredible right after and all game long," Sullivan mentioned after the game.

"As soon as we responded after the goal, I think even when we got scored on, I had full confidence that we would get it done," she noted.

Sullivan's role in controlling the game as the Spirit closed out the first half was notable. She's the longest-tenured player on the active Spirit roster right now, with goalkeeper Aubrey Kingsbury out on maternity leave. Sullivan herself returned to the squad after an ACL injury and then maternity leave. The defensive midfielder completed all of her tackles (three) and aerial challenges (four) and captained the team on the pitch.

In a recent development, "She represents a lot of the values that we want to have as a team, as a club, on and off the field, and right now she's reaching that peak of performance. I'm very, very happy and proud of her because it's been tough for her. Obviously, coming from a long injury, and then maternity leave. So being able to come back to get fit again and try to compete at this level; it's not easy, and she's a role model. An example as a captain with the young players, newly introduced players, and being able to do a lot of things," Spirit head coach Adrian Gonzalez said after the game.

Industry observers note that "Whatever the team needs, she's kind of that voice. Very happy and proud of her because I know what this means to her and also for us. Having her again and being able to play a final is huge for her and for us," he said.

In a recent development, while Utah managed to stave off attacking sequences by the Spirit to close out the opening half, the Spirit's game-winning goal came in the early minutes of the second half. A poor back pass by Utah in their own half was the final dagger. Luvanga pounced on the mistimed pass, and a smart touch inside the box beat goalkeeper Mandy McGlynn.

CLARA LUVANGA POUNCED ON THIS PASS 😮‍💨Her second goal in her second playoff match and the @WashSpirit are one step closer to returning to the @NWSL Final!Watch the semifinal LIVE on @CBS and @paramountplus! pic.twitter.com/f0uUfUU19K.

The Tanzanian international has only been on the roster since September, but her impact on games has grown week to week, and now she can add a game-winning NWSL playoff goal to her resume.

Industry observers note that "It's not the first one that she scores like that. Obviously, she puts a lot of pressure on centerbacks, keepers, and that is very contagious. When you see that your forward is pushing and jumping and pressing like that. Everyone who is behind they follow her, and also creates a lot of doubts and nerves on the opponent team, not facilitating the build-up. And obviously, that was, I think, a massive shot of energy," Gonzalez stated after the game.

In a recent development, "I think it was also a little bit of release, knowing that 'okay, we did the most difficult thing' that was coming back after we conceded a goal, and yeah, happy again because she's bringing a lot. Both attacking and defending, and obviously she's learning so quick and having a huge impact.".

What's next The Spirit will face the winner of Sunday's semifinal between Gotham FC and the Kansas City Current. This will be the Spirit's third consecutive appearance in the NWSL Championship. When the league revealed a neutral site for the 2026 NWSL Championship, it selected Audi Field, and now the Spirit have a chance to play in a home playoff final on Nov. 21.

#59830. How Premier League's big six keep getting richer

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1713 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

How Premier League's big six keep getting richer

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1713 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ten games into the Premier League season, four of the top five places are occupied by 'significant six' clubs.
  • Only second-placed Brighton, a club with a model which must be the envy of many of their rivals, and Premier League ever-presents Everton, have muscled their way in.
  • In pure financial terms, it should come as no surprise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ten games into the Premier League season, four of the top five places are occupied by 'significant six' clubs.

Only second-placed Brighton, a club with a model which must be the envy of many of their rivals, and Premier League ever-presents Everton, have muscled their way in.

In pure financial terms, it should come as no surprise.

The six biggest clubs - Manchester United, Liverpool, Manchester City, Arsenal, Tottenham and Chelsea - now generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the division's other teams.

Industry observers note that and the gap is growing. Every season.

BBC Sport breaks down how the finances of the substantial six have exploded, examines new trends and the impact on the transfer market, and asks how much it really matters.

Recent findings suggest that companies put their money where supporters are prepared to spend it. It is a simple fact of business in every country, a reality of football's food chain.

In England, Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester United traditionally dominated viewing figures, column inches, shirt sales and sponsorship.

Over the past 20 years they have been joined by Chelsea, Manchester City and Tottenham.

This group of clubs now generate so much money it is hard to imagine how they can fail in the long term - even factoring in short-term performance issues.

Let's look at how the gap has grown.

We will use Everton, the only club not in the massive six to be in the Premier League since its inception in 1992.

This tells a tale of how even one of the league's founding members can be left trailing well behind.

It has been revealed that in 2009-10, the gap in revenues between the massive-six average and Everton was Â£120m. In 2024-25, that gap had grown to Â£442m.

So what has driven this huge escalation?

In large part it is the boom in international TV rights.

Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport that it has attracted companies prepared to pay large sums to be associated with the Premier League's top clubs.

"The significant football brand clubs have global fanbases and that makes them very attractive to global commercial partners, especially for sponsorship and front-of-shirt deals," Maguire remarked.

"You combine that with the fact that the Premier League is broadcast to 190 different countries around the world, and especially the international audiences - that allows the clubs to negotiate very good prices.".

Only 10% of Everton's revenue comes from commercial deals, while for the big six it is 45%.

It means Everton, and other clubs in the league, are heavily reliant on broadcast income. It makes up 66% of their revenue.

For Everton at least, this should change following the move to Hill Dickinson Stadium.

But that is unlikely to be enough to stop the gap increasing.

It has taken a few years, but Aston Villa and Newcastle have begun to increase their revenue.

This is largely thanks to the financial rewards of Champions League football.

But even Uefa has created a system which entrenches the position of the biggest clubs.

When the European Super League proposal was torpedoed, Uefa created a new financial deal called the value pillar.

This reserves 35% of all Champions League revenues, or Â£713m, for the historically most successful clubs.

At the end of the league phase last season City are estimated to have earned Â£37.9m from the value pillar, Liverpool Â£35.5m and Chelsea Â£33.3m. Newcastle received only Â£13.6m.

The good news for Villa is their coefficient has improved greatly, aided by last season's Europa League win.

Sources indicate that their value pillar is projected to be worth Â£25m this season. But that will still be less than the big six clubs in the competition.

The cards are stacked against an ambitious club - not just domestically, but in Europe too.

Take a look at the financial trend of the big six and one thing becomes noticeable - Chelsea are beginning to fall behind.

In the past two seasons, and for the first time in recent history, the Blues recorded the lowest revenues of the massive six.

Not just by a small amount. They were Â£74m behind Tottenham, and Â£200m below Liverpool and Manchester City.

City's matchday income is the lowest, with the club's huge revenues largely due to commercial deals.

City, however, have been found guilty of breaching the Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18, inflating the value by using "sham contracts" with sponsors.

The club deny wrongdoing and have lodged an appealed against the verdict.

Chelsea's problem is simple - seats.

Stamford Bridge has a capacity of only 40,000, with no easy scope for expansion. The rest of the major six have grounds which hold at least 60,000.

Chelsea generated an average spend per fan of Â£80 in 2024-25, the second highest in the league after Arsenal.

Yet with 20,000 fewer tickets sold than their big six rivals, Chelsea's total matchday revenues are dwarfed.

"Matchday spend has become increasingly important," Maguire mentioned. "There has been a flatlining of broadcast revenues, especially since 2017.

"As a consequence, clubs have had to look at alternative methods of increasing revenues, especially with costs both on the pitch and off pitch rising so fast.".

Matchday revenue has effectively stalled for Chelsea, rising only Â£16m over the past 10 years. United's has grown by Â£69m and Spurs, thanks to their newly introduced ground, by Â£85m.

Recent findings suggest that "Chelsea are far more reliant upon player sales," Maguire noted. "There is a growing divide because the global appeal is very much aligned with three or four clubs.

"Arsenal have re-established themselves with their progress in the Champions League. Manchester United are a brand in their own right. And Liverpool have expanded Anfield from 44,000 to 61,000, with many of those extra seats having gone to commercial.".

Chelsea's successful player trading model has so far limited the impact.

But there are signs that, financially at least, the substantial six could become the big five.

You might recall that Villa and Newcastle were not fans of the old profit and sustainability rules (PSR).

PSR forced both clubs to sell some of their best players to balance the books.

That has changed this season with squad-cost ratio (SCR).

There is a key difference with SCR, in that it allows a club to spend the money they generate on players. PSR limited losses so was more restrictive.

Sources indicate that "This does make it a little easier for the likes of Villa and Newcastle to spend money," Maguire stated. "But it is still heavily weighted in favour of the major six.

"SCR is different to PSR rather than better. For some people, change is advantageous. For others, it isn't.".

Industry observers note that the big six generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the other clubs. So they can spend hundreds of millions of pounds more on their squads.

This makes the big six even more powerful in the transfer market.

"Look at the clubs who voted against SCR - Brighton, Brentford, Bournemouth, Crystal Palace, Fulham and Leeds," Maguire noted.

"It's very noticeable that those clubs have traditionally been very good at player sales, while they have tended to have lower matchday and commercial revenues.".

Most of the big six - the outlier being Chelsea - are not remotely close to the Premier League's 85% SCR limit.

If you give clubs more money to spend on transfers, the likelihood is they will do just that. And the numbers back that up.

Premier League clubs spent Â£3.5bn - not only a highest total for a summer window, but it almost smashed the record for a whole season, the Â£3.53bn set in 2025-26.

The annual accounting cost of previous transfers, or amortisation, has been rising year on year.

"Over the course of the last decade, transfer amortisation has more than doubled and close to tripled," Maguire remarked.

"Which means that on average, clubs in the Premier League are now spending, or now have a cost which goes into their SCR calculations of just under Â£100m.".

Uefa fears that SCR will make matters worse, and have an inflationary impact across Europe.

And you can see why it is concerned.

In the summer 13 Premier League clubs broke their transfer record.

Brentford, Brighton, Palace, Leeds and Nottingham Forest all spent more than Â£40m on a player - unthinkable until recently.

So we have learned that the big six have more money than ever, and the gap is so huge it is impossible for any other club to compete with them, financially at least.

And this is an vital point: other than Villa and Newcastle, the other clubs are not trying to compete with the significant six.

Clubs like Brentford and Brighton have shown that smart models are just as effective as fat wallets.

They sign the potential stars of the future, nurture them and then sell them to the big six.

Football's ecosystem recycles the significant-six money through the transfer market.

But it is a precarious business for these other clubs.

"The smaller clubs have to get it right on a more regular basis than the bigger clubs," Maguire mentioned.

"The big six can afford to make signings which are Â£60m and Â£70m, who turn out to be relative flops, and still have those players on high wages for several years.".

And this is perhaps the key point about the vast finances of the big six.

Industry observers note that the commercial power of the massive six does not guarantee success. After all, United sit in the relegation zone.

Yet Mauricio Pochettino, their upcoming manager, may well get the chance to revamp the squad despite the club spending Â£945m on players in the past five years.

Industry observers note that the richest clubs can try to spend their way out of trouble. Again and again.

But the rest of the league are only a couple of bad transfer windows from catastrophe.

And that is the real gap between the significant six and the rest.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Plus: more speedy marathons by footballers, headed goals of the season and chairs acting as managers.

Mail us with all of your questions and answers.

“Which club team has had the most international captains playing together at one time?” asks MH Zahid. “Conversely, which international team has had the most club captains in its starting lineup at one time?”.

A quick web search finds a fuss being made in various corners of the internet of Chelsea’s 2009-10 squad because it contained six national team captains in Michael Ballack (Germany), Petr Cech (Czech Republic), Didier Drogba (Côte d’Ivoire), Branislav Ivanovic (Serbia), Mikel John Obi (Nigeria) and John Terry (England). These are, indeed, six people who captained their countries, playing together at one time, but crucially they were not all international captains at that time, which because we like to have our hands bound as tight as possible – no questions please – mean they are disqualified from this particular tournament. Ivanovic, you see, was not named Serbia captain until 2012 and Mikel, who was but a whippersnapper at 22 when the 2009-10 season started, was still seven years from getting his hands on the Nigeria armband.

In a recent development, but if that Chelsea team are not themselves the best answer that Knowledge has come up with, they are at least associated with them, having been knocked out of the Champions League by José Mourinho’s captain-strewn Inter. Inter ended up beating Bayern Munich 2-0 in the final, with a team that included the then full-time captains of Brazil (Lúcio), Romania (Cristian Chivu), Cameroon (Samuel Eto’o) and Macedonia (Goran Pandev), while the captain of Serbia (Dejan Stankovic) came off the bench to replace Chivu in the second half and Pandev was replaced by Sulley Muntari, who while not Ghana’s full-time captain had led the side in their most recent game, a 2-1 defeat at Bosnia and Herzegovina that March.

But that’s not all! Among the unused substitutes was Iván Córdoba, who at this point in his career had lost Colombia’s armband to Mario Yepes but been given it back for their previous game, against Paraguay, in the absence of his fellow centre-back. Also in the team and worthy of note, if not of inclusion in our tally of then captains, were Wesley Sneijder, occasional Netherlands skipper and still their all-time record appearance maker, and Javier Zanetti, who regularly captained Argentina and is No 4 on their list of all-time appearance makers (he would be higher had he not been frozen out by their then manager, Diego Maradona, before the 2010 World Cup), with occasional Kenya captain McDonald Mariga also among the subs.

By our count that’s seven players in one matchday squad who could boast of being their country’s current captain at kick-off, and none of whom captained their club side – that honour went to Zanetti. Our searches have not found another team to match that one, but readers have suggested a couple who came close, in the shape of Tottenham in 2020-21 (who boasted five international captains at the time in Hugo Lloris of France; Serge Aurier of Côte d’Ivoire; South Korea’s Son Heung-min; Gareth Bale of Wales; and England’s own Harry Kane, suggested by John Curry) and Liverpool just last year, when in Conor Bradley, Andy Robertson, Virgil van Dijk, Wataru Endo, Mo Salah and Dominik Szoboszlai they had six – though they never played together while they were all incumbent international captains. Any more for any more?

Industry observers note that the fastest former footballer we found in time for last week’s instalment was Alexei Smertin, the former Russia and Chelsea midfielder, who screamed around the Kazan Marathon course in 2020 in just two hours, 48 minutes and 17 seconds. But as Richard Askham emailed to point out, that has since been bettered by Joe Skarz, formerly of Bury, Rotherham and Oxford United, and current manager of Golcar United of the Northern Counties East League Premier Division, who in 2025 finished the Yorkshire Marathon with a chip time of 2hr 47min 33sec.

The next question is what level of football do you need to reach to qualify as a footballer? Because Stig Lindmark tipped us off about the former AIK academy player Andreas Almgren, whose dreams of football glory were derailed by injury in his teens and eventually shifted his focus towards distance running. In Latest York at the start of this month – while the retired cyclist Tom Dumoulin was putting most former footballers to shame with a time of 2:27:12 – he ran his first ever marathon and only went and won the thing, in 2hr 6min 1sec. With no senior competitive appearances he probably does not count, but it’s a good enough effort to get a mention.

In a recent development, “Has a headed goal ever been awarded goal of the season,” wonders Rupert Sheard. “I can think of a few belters, but awards tend to go to ones kicked in.”.

In a recent development, “The closest I could get was Robin van Persie’s flying header at the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, for the Netherlands against Spain,” writes Sinan Eccles. “He was pipped to the official goal of the tournament by James Rodríguez’s iconic volley, but did make it to third in that year’s Puskas Award – behind Rodríguez and Stephanie Roche.”.

Peter Tomlin writes: “Having researched the goal of the season awards in many countries, the only header I could find that won was Keith Houchen’s fantastic one in the 1986-87 FA Cup Final for Coventry v Tottenham. However, Alisson’s dramatic 95th-minute headed winner v West Brom was voted Liverpool’s goal of the season for the 2020-21 season.”.

And Mark Johnson points out that Basile Boli’s ridiculous bullet header for Marseille against PSG at the end of the 1993 season would surely have won the Ligue 1 goal of the season award but for the inconvenient fact that no such award existed at the time.

Martyn Amos has responded to last week’s scepticism about the possibility of an Ipswich fan website existing in 1990, the year before the first known website went online. “Just to clarify, the original page was set up by Phil Clarke, who was working at BT Labs in Martlesham (near Ipswich), in 1990,” he writes. “At the time, as I mentioned, the web was still experimental, and I think the page was only available internally. Your correspondent is correct in saying that the first public website appeared in August 1991. But the ITFC page still existed, in some recognisable form, using the standard web technology, in 1990, so I think it counts. That’s my understanding, anyway.”.

According to recent reports, with Lee Power taking charge of Swindon Town, in last week’s Knowledge archive we dug up our piece from 2006 on chairs acting as managers, we wrote in October 2015. Neil Bellis, the director of communications at Chester FC, writes to point out we missed Terry Smith off our list.

Sources indicate that “He took over four games into the season despite not really knowing much about ‘soccer’,” writes Neil. “He was a former American Football coach but for some reason ending up buying our club. Not only did we end up getting relegated from the Football League for the first time in 1999-2000 we also saw a few very strange ideas from him including having a team talk as the Lord’s prayer and appointing a captain in defence, midfield and attack. Thankfully we are now fan owned so this level of insanity shouldn’t happen again.”.

One of Smith’s first games as manager was against Aston Villa in the League Cup, a fixture that prompted a visit from ITV to see what was going on. The result of that visit can be seen here:.

“There’s nothing magical about being a coach,’ said Smith not long after his arrival. “It’s like being the general manager of a business, the coaching principles are the same in any sport.” That doesn’t sound too promising but things didn’t really go horribly wrong until the end of November, when Chester began a run of 11 defeats in 12 matches. There’s some footage here of the aftermath of the 5-1 home defeat by Leyton Orient just after Christmas – “I want to thank you guys,” claims Smith in the dressing room. “That’s the most pitiful, pitiful effort I’ve ever damn seen.”.

Smith stepped down as manager and brought in Ian Atkins in January 2000, then sold the club in October 2001.

“What’s the highest score by a team or in a match where no player scored more than one goal?” writes Paul Gage.

“Manchester United have 20 league titles, won by three managers. Liverpool have 20 league titles won by 10. Which teams have the most and fewest titles won by the most and fewest managers?” asks Will Marquand.

Industry observers note that “Djed Spence (shirt No 99) set up Pio Esposito (No 94) in Inter’s 2-0 win over Como at the weekend. Has there ever been a combination for a goal (assist and scorer) with a higher combined shirt number than 193?” writes Joe Strawson.

“Did the Fenerbahce side have more combined Premier League appearances than Liverpool in the teams’ recent Champions League match? If so was this the first instance of a club in Europe playing opposition who had more game appearances in their own league than they had themselves?” ponders Josh Wolff-Martin.

How Berlin's Arab queers are building their community

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (786 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "Adira" is an Arabic slang term used in Levantine queer culture to describe someone with a strong presence — someone powerful and accomplished.
  • In a recent development, it is also the name of a Berlin-based collective that curates events and club nights celebrating the diversity of queer Arab* culture.
  • Among the collective's events is the ADIRA Drag Festival, which celebrated its third edition in Berlin in late October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Adira" is an Arabic slang term used in Levantine queer culture to describe someone with a strong presence — someone powerful and accomplished.

In a recent development, it is also the name of a Berlin-based collective that curates events and club nights celebrating the diversity of queer Arab* culture. The asterisk signals the inclusion of non-Arab ethnic minorities and people with diverse identities and roots in Southwest Asia and North Africa.

Among the collective's events is the ADIRA Drag Festival, which celebrated its third edition in Berlin in late October.

This year's theme, "Who's Your Diva?!," brought together drag performers paying tribute to legendary figures from across the Eastern Mediterranean who have become queer icons — from Egyptian music legend Umm Kulthum to Turkish star Bülent Ersoy and Lebanese pop icon Haifa Wehbe.

Hassandra, co-founder of ADIRA and the ADIRA Drag Festival, was among the performers, taking on the persona of Lebanese pop star Elissa.

According to recent reports, "It is very notable for me to bring my Lebanese Arab identity and culture into what I do, because I think it's a very beautiful culture. And there's a lot of campy, glamorous, beautiful divas," Hassandra remarked.

Elissa's "whole discography is very romantic, raw, soft, kind of like very Adele vibes," Hassandra told DW ahead of the October 30 show. "However, her personality is known to be the extreme opposite. She's very feisty. Very blunt, very unfiltered. Not soft at all as a person.".

The star is also known for speaking out on political issues in Lebanon. She has publicly voiced support for LGBTQ+ communities in the Middle East, while also frequently sparking controversy across the Arab world with her outspoken positions on other political issues.

Hassandra's ADIRA Drag Festival performance addresses this complexity, ultimately "tapping into her sort of controversial political opinions," the drag artist explained.

According to recent reports, this reflects one of the ideas Hassandra hopes to promote with the theme of this year's festival. "As queer people, we tend to idealize a lot of pop divas. But these pop divas are very imperfect in their nature," Hassandra said. The show provides an opportunity to critically revisit these divas' legacy through a more critical lens.

"And this sort of critical lens can be taken into the outside world, as in: never follow anyone in life blindly. No one should follow any politician, any political party, any pop diva, any activist blindly.".

It has been revealed that born in Beirut in 1994, Hassandra studied theater and stage acting at the Lebanese University before moving to Berlin in 2017. "I would say it was it was just a very sort of impulsive decision at the age of 22. I mean, there's no doubt that the economic situation was really bad in Lebanon and continued to become even worse," the artist mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that in Berlin, Hassandra became increasingly involved in the city's independent art scene and queer nightlife. Drag emerged as another form of self-expression for the actor.

Through performances that combine theatrical intensity, political humor, grotesque aesthetics and moments of tenderness, Hassandra challenges conventional understandings of gender and identity.

Sources indicate that their work explores themes of home, nostalgia, displacement and queer Arab culture. These ideas are also central to ADIRA, which Hassandra founded in 2023 with Syrian-German DJ and cultural producer Zuher Jazmati, also known as xanax_attax.

Through panel discussions, performances and music events, ADIRA fosters collective participation and community-building.

As Islamophobia and homophobia rise alongside the far right, spaces like ADIRA offer a sense of belonging and support for Arab queer communities.

That sense of community has become even more key following the deadly Islamist terrorist attack during Berlin's Christopher Street Day pride parade in July.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Industry observers note that in the aftermath, Hassandra felt caught between their different identities. As an Arab queer person, "you fall in this position where then you start receiving a lot of racism," they remarked.

"And I think this is why it's important, for us queer Arabs, to say we are sad over what happened, but that we also reject any of the racism that comes from that," Hassandra remarked. "I think we [the Arab community] are being used in a lot of ways as a punching bag for a lot of things that are happening.".

Recent findings suggest that rather than allowing the attack to fuel hatred and racism, Hassandra noted, "we should make Germany a safer place for everyone to live in."  "There's place for everyone. It's a huge country," they added.

The interview with Hassandra was conducted by Gönna Ketels.

#59824. Super subs, xG kings and $150 million question marks: The Premier League's most intriguing players

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2299 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cbssports ↗ Open Full Page

Super subs, xG kings and $150 million question marks: The Premier League's most intriguing players

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2299 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that whatever you might think about the November international break, there is one fact you simply will not be bothered to argue against: it is well timed for the statistically-minded football fan in your life.
  • Sources indicate that we are not yet, then, at the stage where we can always draw hard and fast conclusions.
  • Industry observers note that spend $100 million on a player who turns 29 next week and the expectation is surely that a player will hit the ground running.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that whatever you might think about the November international break, there is one fact you simply will not be bothered to argue against: it is well timed for the statistically-minded football fan in your life. A 10-game sample size -- that's the useful stuff. At this point, many but not all teams are what their analytics tell us they are. It's similar but not quite the same for players. Not many have hit the 900-minute mark yet, but plenty are at 500-plus, a body of evidence that usually isn't warped by any one good or bad game. Of course, it depends on how good or bad that game is.

Sources indicate that we are not yet, then, at the stage where we can always draw hard and fast conclusions. We are, however, in a position to find some interesting questions. Here are five of them, in player form:.

Industry observers note that spend $100 million on a player who turns 29 next week and the expectation is surely that a player will hit the ground running. That's especially true when they're Bruno Guimaraes, terror of Premier League midfields in a Newcastle United shirt, a player who had long since seemed ready to step up to a Champions League contender. While it would be fair to say that the Brazilian's form is nothing like a problem for table-topping Arsenal, he has not exactly started like a house on fire. Mikel Arteta has acknowledged as much whenever he has spoken about Guimaraes, even when served up the opportunity to praise him after what seemed an impressive performance against Hull City.

Industry observers note that "He's hitting serious levels now, but we can still take him to another level. That's my conviction; I told him that in the dressing room -- he owned a lot of moments in the game, but there is still much more to come." It would be fair to say that, Hull aside, the best levels he has hit have been as a substitute. When he comes off the bench, he passes more accurately, wins more tackles, creates chances and scores brilliant goals. As a starter, he has occasionally looked a beat off his teammates.

According to recent reports, physical data from Gradient Sports hints as to what the issue might be. For every 90 Premier League minutes on the field, Guimaraes covers less of it at sprint speed (≥25 km/h) than any outfield player bar Mikel Merino and spends notably more time jogging than anyone, an average of 30 minutes. Compare Guimaraes to Declan Rice, an admittedly vertiginous bar, and it is easy to see why the new guy looks off the pace.

In a recent development, equally, it explains why he's such a compelling substitute. When the other 21 players on the pitch are flagging, Guimaraes' comparative physical complications go unexposed and he can run the show.

That's all well and good for now, but he can't carry on like this, can he? You would have to assume that Myles Lewis-Skelly will have to make way even if the academy graduate's emergence as a midfield option unlocked an improved Declan Rice at the tail end of last season. The second most expensive signing in your history can't be an impact guy off the bench behind the homegrown kid, right? Probably not, but if there's any team that could justify the idea of Guimaraes as a 12th man, maybe it's Arsenal, where they pride themselves on their game-changing finishers.

Sources indicate that erling Haaland's Swiftian reign at the top of the Premier League xG chart has been interrupted, at least temporarily, by an unlikely source. You'd have to go back to the days of a marauding Romelu Lukaku for the last time an Everton striker looked like they might rule the roost. Only once since the Belgian's departure has an Evertonian cleared 20 goals in all competitions. In the last five, even a dozen has been beyond this club.

Thierno Barry isn't there yet, but boy is he on the right trajectory. His 7.28 non-penalty expected goals (npxG) puts him 0.22 ahead of Haaland and nearly 2.5 npxG up on anyone else in the league. Expand the pool to Europe's top five leagues and he is breathing rarefied air behind the top four of Lamine Yamal, Donyell Malen, Raphinha and Kylian Mbappe, all of whom have the advantage that they are not playing for an upper midtable outfit in the continent's most competitive division. And in that environment, Barry is making the hardest thing in the sport look easy: getting good shots in prime locations.

Industry observers note that if Barry were turning them in as often as he was getting them, Everton might be even higher than sixth. Still, six goals through 10 games is not to be sniffed at, particularly when the pressure on the 24-year-old was so intense. The bungling of a deadline-day move for Folarin Balogun, as Beto moved to Fiorentina, meant it was Barry or bust for David Moyes this season.

In a recent development, perhaps it was an enforced show of faith for a player who was in and out of the XI last season, his first in England, that brought the best out of the former Villarreal man. His manager views the success in more straightforward terms. "He has settled down a bit more," noted Moyes after Barry's brace helped down Coventry. "His language, his understanding, his communication is much better and he has worked hard to get himself in those positions to score.".

Recent findings suggest that it is easy to see why getting the soft factors right might have been all that was required. Barry is the ideal striker for the modern Premier League. Tall, strong and mobile -- he ranks third among center forwards for top speed this season, per Gradient Sports -- he can serve as an outball when a press needs beating and then get in the box. He might not have the technical elegance of an Mbappe, but he makes his presence felt and occupies high-value spaces. That is more valuable than it sounds, as proven when James Tarkowski's howitzer from range deflected in off him. You might not like it, but this is what elite center forward play looks like. Long may it continue, at least as far as Everton are concerned.

According to recent reports, there are three types of underrated footballers. First, your common-or-garden-variety underrated footballers, often to be found plying their trade at Wolverhampton Wanderers or Burnley. Ashley Westwood, in that season, put up stupidly high xA numbers. Then there are the so-often-dubbed-underrated that they actually become a bit overrated. Leighton Baines. Lee Carsley. They don't have to play for Everton, but it does help. Olivier Giroud is another. See, not all Everton.

In a recent development, the most rarely spotted of the underrated is the chameleonic one, correctly pegged for a while, only to develop to the point that he is underrated in a completely different way to how he once was. Take Alex Iwobi. Some time ago, a consensus coalesced around the Nigeria international that he was a good player for a team at Fulham's level (and indeed Everton's). Any minute he was on the field, he would probably be delivering good performances for good Premier League teams.

Industry observers note that not anymore. Ten games in and Iwobi looks like one of the outstanding creative forces in the Premier League, critical to the march towards adequacy that Fulham have undertaken after a slow start to life with Alvaro Arbeloa.

Among true playmakers, Iwobi is one of the best at getting the ball into dangerous areas and creating for his teammates. Iwobi leads the league in expected assists with 2.95 and is tied with Bruno Fernandes for most passes completed into the penalty area. Only Pascal Gross has created more chances.

In a recent development, those players can't match Iwobi when it comes to ball progression either. In terms of advancing the ball not just into the box but from deeper, Fulham's ball-playing fulcrum on the inside left channel has completed more progressive passes than anyone not named Declan Rice or Jan Paul van Hecke.

When Iwobi broke through at Arsenal, he displayed a preternatural sense for how to keep attacks alive, the pass before the pass before the pass. Now a 30-year-old, Iwobi still does that more than he unpicks defenses. One cannot argue, however, that he is not putting his teammates in the right spot. It is just that not everyone quite appreciates how often he does so just yet, including his own supporters, who jeered Iwobi when he was substituted in the early-season defeat to Crystal Palace. Since then, he has responded to his critics in style, teeing up two or more shots in each of Fulham's last seven Premier League matches. If a few more of them had been converted, in fact, if any of them had been converted, then Iwobi might not still be underrated.

The upper reaches of the list of most expensive transfers of all time are hardly all bangers all the time, but of the biggest money moves in the sport's history there are only a handful where at such an early stage you find yourself wondering if anyone really understood what the plan was. Manchester City committed the best part of $150 million on Enzo Fernandez this summer, a fee only eclipsed by Neymar and Kylian Mbappe. Beyond a vague sense that it would be nice to give newly introduced manager Enzo Maresca one of his favorite players, what was it they had in mind?

We pointed out earlier in the season that the aggressive positioning of Fernandez in the 5-3 win over Sunderland looked extreme; at the time it seemed reasonable to view it as a reflection of a stretched-out, chaotic game. Maresca had, of course, unlocked more number 10-ish qualities in the Argentine at Chelsea, but surely that had been reflective of what that team needed, particularly as Cole Palmer went off the boil? Perhaps not. Fernandez keeps popping up in the sort of positions that leave Elliot Anderson on an island. It is one thing to view Anderson as the upcoming Rodri, quite another to immediately throw the England international in at the deep end, tying a whole midfield together by force of will.

Industry observers note that of course you could sketch out a logic for why you might push Fernandez high. It is not so long ago that City deployed two playmakers in front of a sitting midfielder and they ruled the Premier League. Fernandez and Rayan Cherki aren't Kevin De Bruyne and David Silva though.

Maybe Cherki could be offering a level of creation on a par with City greats; he started well enough last season. In year two, he is creating lower-quality chances, his expected assists per 90 dropping by 50%, notably more than the slight uptick in the quality and quantity of shots he is taking. It's no surprise that Cherki is creating less when fewer of his touches are coming in the attacking third. The output has been there so far, five goals and two assists in nine Premier League games, but for that to continue, Maresca might want to be getting his No. 10 into more dangerous spots.

Instead, those seem to be going to Fernandez, who has not proven himself able to get the final-third production to justify his platforming. For every 100 touches he takes, he is delivering significantly less npxG+xA than in either of the previous two seasons. Meanwhile, he is less effective without the ball than he has been at any stage since coming to England. That's no wonder. If an opponent passes through City's frontline, then Fernandez does not have the mobility to get back.

As such, to enable themselves to get perhaps a shot or two more than they would get with Ayyoub Bouaddi or Mateo Kovacic next to Anderson, City have made themselves an even more vulnerable side to the counterattack, already giving up more fast-break openings than they did in 2020-21 or 2021-22. Carry on like this, and Fernandez will become one of those nine-figure transfers, the ones that live in infamy.

It was a signing that delighted a city when it was unveiled in early August, and rightly so. Loaning Carl Rushworth from Brighton had been an inspired bit of business by Coventry City, the then-24-year-old goalkeeper anchoring the best defense in the division as Frank Lampard's side returned to the top flight for the first time in over a quarter of a century. A club-record £22 million fee seemed a snip for such a young talent.

Recent findings suggest that all of that is worth bearing in mind given the struggles Rushworth has endured this season: saving just 53.7% of shots he has faced, conceding 5.19 more goals than the xG value of the shots he has faced. The swagger of last season has been replaced by a sloppiness apparent in both the goals he conceded in the second half against Tottenham, weak gloves doing nothing to repel efforts that came at him a bit quicker and a bit sooner than they might have last year.

Recent findings suggest that none of this needs to be a problem for Rushworth. In 2023-24, James Trafford was another highly touted young goalkeeper afforded a shot at the major time by Burnley. He was obliterated up and down the Premier League, his first touch in the division picking the ball out of the net off Erling Haaland. Those struggles were the making of him, as they have broken others. It'll be some time yet before we discover which way these past few months send Rushworth.

From rotten food to political opponents: Researchers explore how disgust relates to our beliefs, and why the connection is complicated

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1051 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes.
  • But as Americans vote in the US midterm elections, it's time to think about how disgust shapes our politics, or whether our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?
  • The smell of rotten food can make us recoil.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes.

But as Americans vote in the US midterm elections, it's time to think about how disgust shapes our politics, or whether our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

The smell of rotten food can make us recoil. Certain sexual practices can provoke a similar reaction. And in today's polarized political climate, even political opponents can become objects of disgust.

Recent findings suggest that psychologists have long investigated whether sensitivity to disgust helps explain political beliefs. A review of 24 studies found that people who reported being more easily disgusted tended to hold more socially conservative views.

One explanation begins with evolution.

"We think that it evolved in part to reduce exposure to things that could make you sick," psychologist Yoel Inbar, of the University of British Columbia in Canada, told DW.

Industry observers note that but disgust is not a single emotion. The Three-Domain Disgust Scale, developed in 2009, distinguishes three types:.

One theory is that people who are especially wary of germs and disease may also prefer traditional social rules.

Inbar explains that avoiding potential sources of infection can also mean missing out on new experiences.

"Some people are more on the cautious conservative side, and some people are more on the exploring risk-taking side when it comes to pathogen exposure," he said.

In a recent development, indeed, the language of contamination also appears in political rhetoric. During his 2024 presidential campaign, Donald Trump repeatedly described immigrants as "poisoning the blood of our country." Trump has also described himself as a "germaphobe.".

Inbar acknowledges that the evidence linking sensitivity to disgust with conservative political beliefs remains uncertain.

"We have hypotheses. I don't know that we have as strong of evidence as I would like," Inbar said.

Disgust is not exclusively conservative. And what people find revolting can depend on their values.

A 2020 study titled "Is Disgust a "Conservative" Emotion?" found that liberals and conservatives were disgusted by different things.

Conservatives, generally aligned with the Republicans in US politics, reported greater disgust at examples involving sexual behaviors and drug use, while liberals, generally aligned with the Democrats, reported greater disgust at animal abuse and environmental pollution.

However, when asked how easily disgusted they were in general, there was no clear difference across the political spectrum.

Some early studies suggested conservatives indicated stronger physical reactions to frightening or disgusting images, measured partly through changes in sweating.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

But subsequent research, including a 2020 study by political psychologist Bert Bakker at the University of Amsterdam, struggled to reproduce those findings.

Studies based on questionnaires, however, have generally found that people with more conservative attitudes report being more easily disgusted.

"If bodily reactions don't differ across political groups, why do feelings?" Manos Tsakiris, of Royal Holloway and the Centre for the Politics of Feelings at the University of London, told DW.

Tsakiris and colleague Mariana von Mohr wondered whether the answer might lie in how people perceive and interpret signals from their bodies.

Scientists call the perception of internal sensations, such as hunger, breathing or a racing heart, "interoception." It's sometimes called our eighth sense, alongside the familiar five, plus our senses of balance and body position.

"A bodily signal doesn't arrive with a label attached," Tsakiris told DW. "We have to notice it and make sense of it.".

The researchers surveyed 632 US adults, asking how much they noticed and trusted signals from their bodies — a measure known as "interoceptive sensibility.".

They found that people who were more easily disgusted by sexual behavior tended to be more conservative, regardless of how aware they felt of their bodies.

But for moral disgust, the link to conservatism was found only among people who reported lower bodily awareness.

What particularly surprised Tsakiris was that perceived bodily awareness alone had no link to political views.

"People who are highly attuned to their bodies were neither more liberal nor more conservative," he noted.

Inbar questions whether all forms of disgust are equally useful for studying political attitudes.

He and Joshua Tybur, one of the creators of the Three-Domain Disgust Scale, generally prefer measuring pathogen disgust — reactions to potential sources of disease — rather than sexual disgust.

Questions about sexual disgust may already reflect conservative beliefs about sex.

"It's almost asking people the same thing twice," Inbar noted.

The latest study found no significant link between pathogen disgust and conservative views.

In a recent development, inbar wants the findings on bodily awareness and disgust tested again, with predictions set out in advance. For now, he considers them "suggestive at best.".

Tsakiris suggests that people who struggle to understand their bodily feelings may be more vulnerable to political messages telling them what those feelings mean.

Sources indicate that "I know what you're feeling. You're feeling angry or you're feeling disgusted about this thing," he said, illustrating how someone might put an emotional label on another person's unease.

Such labels could influence political behavior, he argues, although the study did not directly test this.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"This is how disgust can do political work: it can turn moral judgments about individuals into judgments about whole groups," he said.

The research cannot establish whether disgust shapes political beliefs or existing beliefs shape what people find disgusting. Bakker notes that political beliefs can influence how people describe their own personalities, suggesting the relationship could work both ways.

"Voting behavior is very complex and citizens make up their mind about politics in a complex way," he told DW.

Industry observers note that inbar also cautions against exaggerating disgust's importance. "The thing to emphasize in your story is that the relationship, while it's consistent, is quite small," he mentioned.

"It's one of the many influences on people's politics.".

Tsakiris advocates what he calls "critical feeling": questioning our emotional responses to provocative material, including social media posts, just as we question the information itself.

He also emphasizes discussing our feelings with others and listening to different perspectives, even when we disagree.

"Life and politics and democracy is a contact sport," he remarked. Edited by: Rosalie Delaney.

#59818. AI is ditching hallucinated references — and other bad habits

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1038 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

AI is ditching hallucinated references — and other bad habits

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1038 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that hallucinated academic citations have become a hallmark of the artificial-intelligence era.
  • The finding is part of an analysis that reports that many LLM tendencies, such as overthinking simple maths problems and complying with illogical requests, fade over time as AI companies release fresh or updated models with improved capabilities.
  • “We, as users of these systems, need to not have such a fixed view of what AI can do and what it can’t do,” says co-author Owen Queen, an AI researcher at Stanford University in California.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Credit: FabrikaSimf/Shutterstock.

Industry observers note that hallucinated academic citations have become a hallmark of the artificial-intelligence era. But they might soon be gone for good. Researchers have found that the latest large language models (LLMs) rarely, if ever, attribute information to sources that don’t exist.

The finding is part of an analysis that reports that many LLM tendencies, such as overthinking simple maths problems and complying with illogical requests, fade over time as AI companies release fresh or updated models with improved capabilities. Many of these tendencies disappear about 16 months after the phenomenon is first described in a published paper. The analysis, described in a blog post, has not been peer reviewed.

“We, as users of these systems, need to not have such a fixed view of what AI can do and what it can’t do,” says co-author Owen Queen, an AI researcher at Stanford University in California.

Sources indicate that but just because an LLM behaviour fades as models improve doesn’t mean that the effect immediately disappears, says Maxim Topaz, a health-care AI researcher at Columbia University in New York City. Topaz has found1 that the number of hallucinated citations in academic papers has risen drastically since 2023, probably because more researchers than ever before are using LLMs, and they often aren’t using the latest models.

Industry observers note that queen and his colleague identified 50 widely cited LLM behaviours that were described in publications between late 2022, when some of the first LLMs became widely available, and late 2025. They then gave the same prompts that first elicited the behaviour in the original publications to 20 LLMs that were released from mid-2024 to late 2026 to see if the effect has strengthened or weakened over time. For example, they asked each model to count the number of r’s in ‘strawberry’ — something that LLMs have found difficult but can now do more reliably.

Sources indicate that nearly half of the behaviours they checked have largely disappeared from newer models, leading the researchers to deem those effects ‘expired’. Expired behaviours had an average lifespan of about 16 months after publication, although some were fleeting — models stopped overthinking simple maths problems just a month and a half after this tendency was published. Other traits persisted, such as the stereotyping of Black women by disproportionately describing them as resilient, which lasted for longer than three years.

In a recent development, although most of the retested LLM behaviours have faded over time, three have become more pronounced. Today’s models praise what their users like even more often than they used to, LLMs more strongly favour their own writing compared with that of other LLMs and people; and LLMs are now even worse than they used to be at generating truly random numbers.

Industry observers note that in a 2023 study2, OpenAI’s GPT-3.5 hallucinated 55% of citations when asked to write literature reviews. Models have, on average, fabricated fewer citations over time since then, but the newest model in the latest analysis — GPT-6.1 Sol — was the only one to hallucinate zero citations. Still, the researchers deemed this behaviour to be expired as of April because the latest models hallucinate very few citations.

It has been revealed that this decline in hallucinations is not yet reflected in published papers. Earlier this year1, Topaz and his colleagues analysed 2.5 million biomedical papers published between early 2023 and early 2026 and found that the rate of hallucinated citations had increased 12-fold. Topaz says that researchers are increasingly using LLMs and that papers published in 2026 were probably written in 2025 or earlier with models that were more hallucination-prone.

Research suggesting that LLM behaviours have expired might oversimplify reality, claims Maarten Sap, an AI researcher at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.

Recent findings suggest that LLMs often have different training and optimization processes, Sap notes, and it’s possible that some of the models tested in this research had training that was better suited to avoiding these behaviours than did others. Understanding how each model was trained in relation to the prompts could yield more specific insights into LLM capabilities, says Sap. “Whether they can do a certain thing is less interesting to me than why they are doing it.”.

WSL talking points: Chelsea’s gamble pays off and have Arsenal lost fear factor?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1137 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Blues beat champions after bold substitution and Gunners’ home struggles continue with fifth consecutive WSL draw.
  • Sonia Bompastor attempted to deflect suggestions that the removal of Kadeisha Buchanan 12 minutes into Chelsea’s top-of-the-table clash with Manchester City was tactical, but few were convinced by the claim that it was down to injury.
  • It has been revealed that manchester United earned their fourth clean sheet in all competitions in their 2-0 defeat of Crystal Palace.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Blues beat champions after bold substitution and Gunners’ home struggles continue with fifth consecutive WSL draw.

Sonia Bompastor attempted to deflect suggestions that the removal of Kadeisha Buchanan 12 minutes into Chelsea’s top-of-the-table clash with Manchester City was tactical, but few were convinced by the claim that it was down to injury. The manager noted the centre-back, who had not asked to come off and walked straight down the tunnel, had taken a knock to the head in training and been assessed and cleared, but that during the game “she was not herself”. On came Veerle Buurman and the threat of Khadija Shaw was nullified, the Dutch defender restricting the golden boot favourite so well that Shaw did not manage a shot on target. Bompastor said after the game that she had not spoken to Buchanan but that she would “explain myself to her”. “I always have good relationships with the players, bring them clarity, and I’m always direct and honest so they have the information,” she said. “It won’t be any different.” Enforced or not, the substitution was a huge gamble that paid off, even after the loss of Melvine Malard to injury in the first half reduced their number of remaining in-game substitution windows to one. Suzanne Wrack.

Match report: Chelsea 1-0 Manchester City.

It has been revealed that manchester United earned their fourth clean sheet in all competitions in their 2-0 defeat of Crystal Palace. Maya Le Tissier stole the headlines with her goal on her 150th appearance for the club but the team’s improved defensive stability is also catching the eye and the centre-back is key to that. “For a defender you expect as the minimum you need to defend well and help to build,” said the head coach, Eva Olid. “But now she’s scoring goals and that is more than a manager can ask from a centre-back. She’s in a high level and I’m so happy for her.” Le Tissier is showing consistent solidity and appears to be enjoying life under Olid now that things have settled, after seven goals conceded in their opening two WSL games. United have conceded four in eight WSL games since and are starting to show their flair. SW.

Recent findings suggest that have teams stopped fearing Arsenal at the Emirates Stadium? Their run of five consecutive WSL draws at home suggests so. London City Lionesses had 56% possession on Sunday and controlled the game for significant spells, especially in the second half, and although Arsenal created the greater chances, they do not play with the aura of a side attracting the largest attendances in the division. Renée Slegers was asked whether she was worried her team were losing that home “fear factor” and mentioned: “No, because we love playing at the Emirates. We had the biggest crowd so far in the season, the atmosphere was fantastic under the lights.” Probed further about her side’s home form, the head coach said: “I don’t think we’ve lost the fear factor, I think it’s a very hard place for oppositions to come.” Her side host West Ham next Sunday, looking for that elusive home WSL win. Tom Garry.

Match report: Arsenal 1-1 London City.

Tottenham Hotspur were the latest team frustrated by Everton’s defensive solidity as they were held to a goalless draw. Despite controlling the ball and registering 17 shots, only three efforts were on target as they failed to score for the first time. Martin Ho was keen to highlight their opponents’ strengths as a key reason. “When we got into that attacking third, it was going to take something really special,” he told Spursplay. “They defended so deep with so many numbers behind the ball. You’re waiting for one of those moments to drop.” It was just the kind of performance fans have come to expect from Scott Phelan’s side. Unbeaten in their past three, in which they have faced Manchester United, Chelsea and Spurs, Everton have developed a strong resilience and character in recent weeks. Where they struggle is at the other end. Everton have scored eight goals this season (three of them own goals), higher than only Charlton in the WSL. Sophie Downey.

Liverpool ended their five-game winless league run with a statement victory over struggling Brighton, their third away win in 17 games. It has been a frustrating October and November block for Gareth Taylor and his team so there was much relief on the sideline that they were finally able to turn performance and opportunity into three points. Liverpool had less of the ball but their fast counterattacking proved too much for the Seagulls. A significant key to their success was Beata Olsson. She has six goals from her past five games in all competitions, stepping up when her team have needed it most. Injuries have kept out Aurélie Csillag and Ceri Holland for the best part of the season and Sophie Roman Haug is recovering from an anterior cruciate ligament injury sustained 13 months ago. With limited attacking options, therefore, it will be very welcome that the Swedish striker has found her form in front of goal. SD.

In a recent development, viviane Asseyi continued her impressive scoring form with a superb brace in West Ham’s 2-0 victory over Charlton, taking her WSL tally to seven this season. The striker opened the scoring with a composed finish from the edge of the area before producing the standout moment of the afternoon, curling a spectacular 25-yard free-kick into the top corner beyond Charlton’s goalkeeper, Anna Koivunen. Asseyi could have completed a hat-trick but her two goals proved decisive. West Ham’s head coach, Rita Guarino, described her as “an important player”, adding that Asseyi was in a good goalscoring spell. Guarino felt Asseyi could have been happier with a hat-trick, but her latest double underlines her importance to West Ham’s attacking threat. Mitul Samji.

Recent findings suggest that poor officiating dominated the narrative of the second city derby as Aston Villa edged Birmingham City 1-0, with both sides feeling hard done by. First, City felt Lucy Parker had fouled Océane Hurtré in the penalty area in the 24th minute, only for the referee to award a corner. Whether the incident was inside the box was disputable, but it did appear to be a foul. Minutes later, Villa had a goal from Océane Deslandes overruled for what was declared a foul on the goalkeeper in another contentious call, but they managed to find a winner in the second half. The decisions added to growing concerns about consistency in the WSL. Ho recently suggested officiating had worsened, and matches such as this do little to ease those concerns. Before VAR is introduced, improving the quality of refereeing must be a priority to avoid undermining the league’s standards and progress. Réshma Rao.
